entry.title: Naming the episodic race leaderboard boards, part 29
entry.summary: All 150 functions in this batch were named: they are the same nine leaderboard accessor methods instantiated once per race board, continuing the run of earlier naming lanes without a single variant.
entry.content:
All 150 functions in this batch were named: they are the same nine leaderboard accessor methods instantiated once per race board, continuing the run of earlier naming lanes without a single variant.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, which turned out to be leaderboard info classes for seventeen ranked episodic race boards.

What was found

  • Verified Every method slot has exactly one code shape across all its instances, and each slot matches the same-named method from the previous batch exactly, so the existing names transfer.
  • Verified Each board's name method returns its own board-name string and each id method returns a small integer that runs linearly with the race number; a value the previous lane predicted was confirmed on first read.
  • Verified One full board group read end to end behaves as described before: id search, id lookup, size and kind switches, mapped-index search, id mapping, and a nineteen-column row pack loop with a presence bitmask.
  • Verified This batch has none of the dual class tags the previous lane found on id stubs, which is exactly what its linker-folding explanation predicts for this id range: a confirmed negative control.
  • Verified A class-record cross-check puts all nine batch addresses in the board's virtual table with slot numbers equal to table indices, seconding the previous lane's correction note.

What was decided or recommended

All 150 functions keep the family's existing nine method names, with high confidence for the string- and constant-returning methods and medium for the behaviour-derived ones. The next batch should contain the final board's last two methods. The shared helper routines and shared table slots are still unnamed and would help future lanes cite callers.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function through the executable's memory-mapped image, group by code shape, resolve the string pointers behind the name stubs, and compare each group's shape against the previous batch's same-named methods before reusing the names.

What was confusing or went wrong

Nothing went wrong. The inventory labels only some of the name and kind stubs with slot numbers, but the labelled and unlabelled copies are code-identical, so the labels transfer safely.

entry.title: Naming the episodic race leaderboard methods, and shared constant stubs
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive leaderboard methods were all named with the established family vocabulary, and fourteen constant-return stubs turned out to be genuinely shared between the leaderboard classes and unrelated task classes through linker folding.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive leaderboard methods were all named with the established family vocabulary, and fourteen constant-return stubs turned out to be genuinely shared between the leaderboard classes and unrelated task classes through linker folding.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of one hundred fifty consecutive unnamed game functions, which inventory hints attributed to ranked episodic race leaderboard info classes.

What was found

Verified The batch holds the tail of one race class, sixteen complete nine-method groups, and the head of the next class. Every method slot shows exactly one code shape across all its instances, with zero variants.

Verified The name methods each return a pointer to their own board name string, and the id methods each return a small integer that every sibling method passes as a key to one shared board-data helper. Board ids run consecutively with no gaps, confirming the previous lane's predicted value for the first race in this batch.

Verified Fourteen of the seventeen id stubs are also referenced by task class virtual tables at the same slot. A task class slot outside the batch decodes to the same return-a-constant shape, so that task slot is a per-class integer getter. The two class systems share one copy of each identical six-byte body.

Inferred The sharing is linker identical-function folding: the task type numbers happen to equal the board numbers, so the linker kept a single copy. The three id stubs with no task counterpart are exactly the values with no matching task number.

Verified The class record for one race in this batch points nine virtual table slots at exactly the nine batch addresses, and the inventory virtual-function numbers match those slot indices directly.

What was decided or recommended

All one hundred fifty functions were named with the nine established family method names: thirty-three at high confidence where a string or cross-checked integer pins the meaning, and one hundred seventeen at medium where the behaviour is verified but the wording follows precedent. Nothing was left unnamed.

Naming lanes should treat dual virtual-table tags on constant-return stubs as real code sharing, not as inventory errors. The names stand because the bytes do what both callers need.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each batch function through the mapped executable image and cluster by mnemonic sequence per slot; read the board-name strings and board-id integers; cross-check that every sibling passes its own id to the shared board-data helper; compare the virtual-table targets in the class records for both the leaderboard and task families.

What was confusing or went wrong

An early cross-check script looked for the id key only in the first six instructions and flagged dozens of mismatches; the key is loaded slightly later in three of the slot shapes. Reading one full method group end to end cleared it up. A previous report described the inventory slot numbers as offset by three from the class record indices, but the record checked here matches them directly.

entry.title: Re-running a verified batch caught a real bug, and black box was not enough to fix it
entry.summary: This lane re-ran another lane's five verified input-handling functions with fresh random seeds and the per-function wrong versions the current brief requires. Four passed unchanged. The fifth failed three trials out of twelve hundred, all on the sign bits of not-a-number values, and the cause was the compiler reordering floating point operations behind the rewrite's back. Fixing it took two attempts and taught the project that the usual black box trick does not always hold.
entry.content:
This lane re-ran another lane's five verified input-handling functions with fresh random seeds and the per-function wrong versions the current brief requires. Four passed unchanged. The fifth failed three trials out of twelve hundred, all on the sign bits of not-a-number values, and the cause was the compiler reordering floating point operations behind the rewrite's back. Fixing it took two attempts and taught the project that the usual black box trick does not always hold.

What was asked

Rewrite five neighbouring input-handling functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the checker, running at least a thousand trials per function plus one deliberately wrong version per function that must fail. The batch turned out to duplicate an earlier lane's finished batch, so this lane became an independent re-verification: same rewrites rebuilt from source, new random seeds, and the missing wrong versions added.

What was found

Verified Four of the five functions passed twelve hundred fresh trials each with zero failures, and all five wrong versions failed as required, which confirms the contracts can tell right from wrong.

Verified The fifth function failed three trials out of twelve hundred with a new seed after passing twelve hundred with the old seed. All three failures were not-a-number sign and payload bits only, in three different spots of one computation. Reading the compiled rewrite showed the compiler had rewritten a multiply-then-add as a subtract in the opposite order, commuted two multiplies, and commuted one add. Each change is invisible for ordinary numbers but picks a different not-a-number when both operands are special values.

Verified The first fix attempt, routing every operation through helpers that hide both operands in black boxes, fixed the three known failures but the compiler then merged the two remaining twin additions into one paired instruction with the operands swapped, which two further trials caught. The second fix attempt also fenced each helper off from inlining, so every operation is now an opaque call that must compile to one scalar instruction in the original's order. The final machine code was read to confirm this, and the function then passed twelve hundred trials with the wrong version still failing.

Inferred Any float-heavy rewrite whose only evidence is a passing trial run may hide the same kind of latent reordering, since the first twelve hundred trials showed nothing. Re-running with a fresh seed is a cheap way to shake such cases out.

What was decided or recommended

  • Float operation order in rewrites should be pinned with never-inlined black box helpers, not black box alone, whenever two similar operations sit near each other and the compiler could merge them.
  • Re-running finished functions with fresh seeds is worth doing: it found a genuine defect here at low cost.
  • The fixed rewrite supersedes the earlier lane's version of that one function; the other four are unchanged.

How to reproduce it

Build the lane's rewrite crate for 32-bit Windows with panics set to abort, copy the resulting library next to the lane's contracts, and run the lane's copy of the checker driver once per contract with the stock worker. Each contract runs twelve hundred trials for the rewrite and up to a hundred for its wrong version. The float-order defect shows as a small number of call-comparison failures flagged by the checker's not-a-number diagnostic, all in the staged-descriptor snapshot of the solver-probe function.

What was confusing or went wrong

The most confusing moment was the second fix failing: the black box pattern is the project's recommended way to pin float order, and it looked airtight, yet the compiler merged the two additions anyway. It took reading the compiled output instruction by instruction to see the paired instruction with swapped lanes. The lesson is that black box hides values from the optimizer but does not stop it from pairing two identical-looking operations, which is exactly what the no-inline fence prevents.

entry.title: Three traps from verifying user interface text routines
entry.summary: A production batch of five user interface functions verified three and surfaced three traps that will bite other lanes: a float-branch translation that is wrong only for NaN, rewrite builds that need frame pointers when callees leave deliberate stack residue, and a near-twin function whose loop has no exit guard.
entry.content:
A production batch of five user interface functions verified three and surfaced three traps that will bite other lanes: a float-branch translation that is wrong only for NaN, rewrite builds that need frame pointers when callees leave deliberate stack residue, and a near-twin function whose loop has no exit guard.

What was asked

Rewrite five medium-sized input-ui functions in Rust and prove each equivalent to the original with the checker: two text-fitting routines that truncate strings with an ellipsis, one text container refresh routine, and two larger constructor-style routines.

What was found

  • Verified Take-if-below after a float compare is taken when the operands are unordered. A rewrite that rendered it as a negated ordered compare matched on every finite input but kept a NaN where the original kept it too only after the branch was written the other way round. The exact pairs are: take-if-below means not-above-or-equal, take-if-above means ordered-above. Every float jump must be checked against the NaN row, not just the ordered rows.
  • Verified One routine calls helpers with deliberately unbalanced cleanup: one pops nothing while taking a stack word, another pops eight words while taking three, and the leftover bytes sit on the frame until a later call consumes them. Rust function types assume cleanup matches the argument count, so the compiler's stack tracking drifted from reality and later argument setup read wrong slots. The failure appeared only in the call log while everything else passed. Building the rewrite crate with forced frame pointers fixes it with no change to observable behaviour.
  • Verified The two text-fitting routines look like twins but their shrink loops differ: one guards a shrinking length with signed compares, the other loops purely on the width compare with unsigned compares and no guard. Constant scripted widths make the unguarded original loop without end and corrupt its own tables, so its proof drives the width down per call the way the running game would.

What was decided or recommended

  • Verified Three functions verified at one thousand trials each with per-function wrong versions that fail as required. The two largest functions were deferred with retry kits: their call inventories, cleanup values, and contract sketches are recorded for the next lane.
  • Inferred The checker's call-mismatch display shows only the first three calls with no truncation marker, which made a late difference look like two identical logs. A first-difference index in the stock display would save significant debugging time.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's three contracts with the stock worker and read the verdicts: each shows one thousand passing trials, full branch-shape coverage, and a failing wrong version. Rebuilding the rewrite crate without forced frame pointers reproduces the container routine's call-log failure within sixty trials.

What was confusing or went wrong

The container routine's first full-path failure presented as two identical three-call logs that still failed, because the display truncates after three calls. A display-only debug worker build showed the real difference at the twenty-second call. Separately, an early assumption that the twin routines shared control flow cost one full contract run before a careful diff showed the missing guard.

entry.title: Naming a leaderboard template family: nine methods, one vocabulary
entry.summary: All 150 functions in this batch turned out to be the same nine virtual methods repeated once per ranked race leaderboard, and every one could be named with the vocabulary earlier lanes had already established for sibling boards.
entry.content:
All 150 functions in this batch turned out to be the same nine virtual methods repeated once per ranked race leaderboard, and every one could be named with the vocabulary earlier lanes had already established for sibling boards.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first and naming each function in project style with a confidence level.

What was found

Verified The batch holds ranked episodic race leaderboard descriptors, each exposing the same nine methods in the same order. Two return constants: one returns the board's display name string and the other its small integer board id. The rest look up column metadata: find a column's index by id, fetch an id by index, resolve a column's byte size and type tag, two mapped-index lookups, and one routine that loops over all nineteen columns packing a row.

Verified Every slot's instruction shape is identical across all groups, and each board id matches the lookup key its eight siblings pass to the shared board-data helper. Board ids rise with race number but skip fourteen values midway through the batch, suggesting other leaderboard types sit between these races.

Verified The method wording matches what earlier naming lanes chose for hundreds of sibling leaderboard classes, including the immediately preceding race groups, so names stay consistent across the family.

What was decided or recommended

All 150 functions were named, about one in five at high confidence (the name and id getters, pinned by a string and an integer respectively) and the rest at medium confidence (behaviour read from the code, wording following family precedent). Future naming lanes hitting this template family should reuse the same nine names: the reliable signals are the name string for the name getter, the small integer also used as a lookup key for the id getter, and the fixed nine-slot address order per board.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble one full nine-function group through the executable's mapped image, collect each function's callees, referenced strings and mnemonic shape into a table, and compare against the already-named sibling boards in the merged lane names. A per-slot uniformity check over the whole batch plus a check that each id getter's constant equals the key its siblings use confirms the pattern before naming.

What was confusing or went wrong

An early uniformity check falsely flagged two slots as differing across groups: the evidence script had disassembled a few bytes past each function's end into an inline jump table. The real code was identical; only the trailing bytes decoded as nonsense differed. Truncating disassembly at each function's stated size fixed the comparison.

entry.title: Leaderboard naming, third round: the same nine methods, new boards
entry.summary: All 150 functions in this batch turned out to be the same nine leaderboard-info methods already named for two earlier board families, repeated once per board across seventeen episodic race boards, so every function got a name by verifying the code skeletons matched and reusing the established method names.
entry.content:
All 150 functions in this batch turned out to be the same nine leaderboard-info methods already named for two earlier board families, repeated once per board across seventeen episodic race boards, so every function got a name by verifying the code skeletons matched and reusing the established method names.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive unnamed functions, using strings, imports, known callers, class tables and data flow as evidence, with a confidence per name.

What was found

Verified Each board implements the same nine virtual methods with byte-identical instruction skeletons across all seventeen boards, differing only in a board-id constant.

Verified All nine skeletons are identical to the ones an earlier lane analyzed for a different board family, so its nine method names were reused: board name, board id, find column index, get column id, get column size, get column kind, get mapped column index, map column id, and pack row.

Verified Board ids run sequentially with the board number and every same-board method passes the same id to a shared schema helper, which confirms the board-id names two independent ways. One board's id getter is an encrypted stub instead of cleartext, but its id is still established by its eight sibling methods.

Verified The batch ends mid-board: the last board's final two methods belong to the next batch and their skeletons were pre-confirmed.

What was decided or recommended

Named all 150 functions, 33 at high confidence and 117 at medium, none left empty. The next naming lane covering leaderboard boards should keep reusing these nine names after diffing skeletons first, and should expect the inventory's subsystem label to be wrong for this range.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function through the mapped executable image, group by instruction skeleton per table slot, read each board's virtual table to attribute unnamed entries, extract the board-id immediate each method passes to the shared helper, and compare skeletons against the earlier analyzed family before reusing its names.

What was confusing or went wrong

Nothing went wrong. The main surprise was how completely mechanical the batch was once the pattern was recognized: one skeleton per slot held across all seventeen boards with no exceptions.

entry.title: Naming a leaderboard template family by its constants
entry.summary: One batch of 150 unnamed functions turned out to be a single family: the virtual methods of seventeen ranked episodic-race leaderboard specializations, one per race, each repeating the same slots with only a board id constant changed. All 150 were named, most at high confidence.
entry.content:
One batch of 150 unnamed functions turned out to be a single family: the virtual methods of seventeen ranked episodic-race leaderboard specializations, one per race, each repeating the same slots with only a board id constant changed. All 150 were named, most at high confidence.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first and then naming each function with a confidence level.

What was found

Verified Every function in the batch is a virtual method of a ranked episodic-race leaderboard info object, races 88 through 104. Each race repeats the same nine method shapes: return the board id, return the board name string, find an index by id, fetch a row by index, query a column width, query an entry kind, reverse-search a row position, look up a value by id, and serialize a row. Board ids run sequentially with the race number, and each name method returns that race's own leaderboard name string.

Verified Sixteen functions the inventory listed as unknown with no vtable evidence are the entry-kind method for sixteen of the races: their jump tables map classifier results to kind codes exactly as the already-verified entry-kind method does. Another seventeen unknown functions are the name methods, each returning its race's leaderboard string.

Inferred The largest method in each set, about three hundred bytes, encodes a full nineteen-column leaderboard row into caller buffers with a presence mask. Its exact role is read from the code but the wording of the name is ours, so it is the only method kept at medium confidence.

What was decided or recommended

Names use the full leaderboard class with the race number plus a method name, so all 150 names are unique and later tools can tell races apart. The subsystem for the whole family is the online network code, not the pedestrian task cluster label the inventory carried. A later lane with a running copy should name the two shared table helpers, whose bytes are encrypted on disk and whose roles are known only through previously verified rewrites.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble one instance of each size group through the mapped executable image, extract the board id constant and any referenced strings per function, compare jump tables across instances, and check each shape against the verified rewrites of the same virtual slots from sibling leaderboard specializations. Scripts and per-function evidence tables are kept in the lane scratch folder.

What was confusing or went wrong

An early evidence script read past the end of each function and credited one function with the next function's string, briefly suggesting the row serializer referenced a leaderboard name. Constraining every scan to the function's own byte range removed the false references. Earlier automated names for these slots had copied the template header as the name, which looked meaningful at a glance but named nothing.

entry.title: A proximity scan that reads its own uninitialized stack
entry.summary: One input-ui scan function initializes only seven of eight entries in each of three working arrays, then loops over all eight, so every pass reads three words of uninitialized stack; the proof pins them to zero and passes.
entry.content:
One input-ui scan function initializes only seven of eight entries in each of three working arrays, then loops over all eight, so every pass reads three words of uninitialized stack; the proof pins them to zero and passes.

What was asked

Rewrite three neighboring input-ui functions in Rust and prove each equivalent to the original with the checker, including one large no-argument scan over entity records.

What was found

Verified The scan keeps three eight-slot working rows (distances, row tags, chain links) but its setup writes only the first seven slots of each; the eighth slot of every row is never stored before the ranking loop reads all eight. Only one of the three garbage words is observable downstream, as an argument to a ranking call; the other two are overwritten or dropped before anything compares them.

Verified The function's listed size cuts its final block mid-instruction; nine bytes past the listed end hold one more store and the loop-back jump, which the rewrite includes.

Verified A global the scan reads twice in a row is an index into itself (first word selects one of the following words as the record pointer), not a heap pointer; planting a pointer there faults, planting the small index passes.

What was decided or recommended

The contract sets a defined zero fill for uninitialized stack, and the rewrite hard-codes zeroes for the three eighth slots, matching the original exactly under that fill. Later lanes should check any fixed-count setup loop against the loop bound it feeds: a seven-write setup feeding an eight-read loop is easy to copy wrong.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the scan function and count the setup stores against the eight-iteration ranking loop; run the checker contract for it with and without the stack fill and compare the eighth ranking call's second argument.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first contract faulted on exactly the trials where the self-indexed table was dereferenced, which first looked like a bad heap link; dumping one trial's fault record showed the index register held a pointer-sized value, which pointed at the table shape. A later mismatch showed two pairs of table values swapped, which traced to misreading a lane-interleave instruction as concatenation. Both are recorded here so the next lane recognizes the signatures.

entry.title: Naming ranked race leaderboard methods, boards 71 to 88
entry.summary: All 150 functions in this batch were named with the established nine-method leaderboard vocabulary, re-verified slot by slot, and two new variants turned up: one board keeps its id stub in a padding gap the inventory never listed, and several id stubs carry a second reference from a descriptor record rather than a foreign table.
entry.content:
All 150 functions in this batch were named with the established nine-method leaderboard vocabulary, re-verified slot by slot, and two new variants turned up: one board keeps its id stub in a padding gap the inventory never listed, and several id stubs carry a second reference from a descriptor record rather than a foreign table.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, which turned out to be per-board virtual methods of the ranked episodic race leaderboard template for boards 71 through 88.

What was found

Verified every function falls into one of nine single-skeleton slots already named by earlier lanes: board name, board id, find column index, get column id, get column size, get column kind, mapped column index, map column id, and pack row. Table position proved the slot of every unattributed entry, and each board's methods agree on exactly one board id with zero conflicts.

Verified three boards have no per-board id stub in the batch, in two different ways. Two point their fourth table slot at per-board stubs in the encrypted region, matching a pattern an earlier lane reported. The third points at a genuine id stub in clear code that sits in padding bytes between two inventoried functions and has no inventory entry of its own.

Verified ten id stubs have a second reference outside their own table. The neighbours are a fixed pair of shared addresses in all ten cases, not the sibling methods a foreign table would hold, so these are per-board descriptor records referencing the id stub, not linker-folded sharing between tables.

Inferred the descriptor records are leaderboard registration entries; their exact layout is unknown. Unknown the exact contracts of the two shared encrypted helpers every schema method calls.

What was decided or recommended

  • All 150 names reuse the inherited nine-method vocabulary with per-board class qualification; 31 at high confidence, 119 at medium, none left empty.
  • Check the neighbours of any double reference before calling it folded sharing: a fixed neighbour pair means a descriptor record, sibling methods mean a table.
  • The next lane on this family should name the last board's remaining eight methods first, then continue upward, keeping the skeleton and id-unanimity checks.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each batch function through the memory-mapped image, group by code skeleton with immediates stripped, read one full disassembly per slot, extract the board id immediate each method passes to the shared schema helper, and scan read-only data for pointers to each function to prove table slots and count references.

What was confusing or went wrong

One verification command printed a long result that arrived truncated, confirming most but not all copies of a loop bound. A second script that printed only a pass or fail summary confirmed all copies cleanly. Compact summaries beat long prints for machine checks.

entry.title: Naming 150 leaderboard methods: board ids run sequential again
entry.summary: Verified All 150 functions in this batch were named as per-board leaderboard methods for episodic ranked-race boards 54 to 71, and every board id measured extends a simple rule: the id equals 203 plus the board number.
entry.content:
Verified All 150 functions in this batch were named as per-board leaderboard methods for episodic ranked-race boards 54 to 71, and every board id measured extends a simple rule: the id equals 203 plus the board number.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, which the inventory attributed to one template family of per-board leaderboard info classes, with 30 entries carrying no inventory name at all.

What was found

Verified The batch holds 16 complete nine-method blocks plus a five-method head for board 54 and a one-method tail for board 71. Every method was confirmed against its class virtual table re-read from the executable image, with zero mismatches, and each table slot has exactly one code shape shared by all boards.

MethodCountBehaviour
get_board_name16returns the board name string
get_board_id17returns the board id constant
find_column_index17linear search of the id array, index or -1
get_column_id17array element by position, or -1
get_column_size17column type to byte width
get_column_kind17column type to kind code
get_mapped_column_index17map through one list, search in another
map_column_id16paired-list id translation
pack_row16row builder over 19 column positions

Verified Board ids for boards 54 to 71 are sequential, 257 to 274. This is the second board range where the id-equals-203-plus-number rule holds exactly; an earlier batch found it for boards 21 to 24 and scattered ids for boards 25 to 37. Three batch members are independently verified rewrites whose documentation matches the chosen names exactly.

Unknown Why the id rule holds in some board ranges and scatters in others, and what owns a handful of orphaned schema ids seen by an earlier lane.

What was decided or recommended

The earlier lanes' nine-name vocabulary was reused unchanged so merged names stay consistent; 33 names carry high confidence and 117 medium. The next naming lane on this family should keep recording per-board ids until the orphaned schema ids are claimed, and can name mechanically from slot plus board with spot-check reads.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function from the memory-mapped image, group by code shape, confirm each against its class virtual table, and read the board id constant and name string per board. The lane scripts gather, verify and build the names file in that order.

What was confusing or went wrong

Nothing went wrong. The only wrinkle was the 30 inventory-unnamed entries, which resolved cleanly: the six-byte ones return their board's name string and the rest share the column-kind code shape and sit in the matching virtual-table slot.

entry.title: Twenty startup registration helpers verified, two checker gaps mapped
entry.summary: Verified A batch of twenty small neighbouring startup functions, all shaped as initialise-then-register pairs, was rewritten in Rust and each rewrite passed eleven hundred differential trials against the original with its deliberately wrong version caught every time.
entry.content:
Verified A batch of twenty small neighbouring startup functions, all shaped as initialise-then-register pairs, was rewritten in Rust and each rewrite passed eleven hundred differential trials against the original with its deliberately wrong version caught every time.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty small timing-subsystem functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the version four checker, one wrong version per function included.

What was found

  • Verified The batch is one family: most functions run a subsystem initialiser and then hand a callback to a registrar; a few initialise a lock object through a system import slot, two fold a performance-counter reading into stored values, one zeroes a 256-entry table record by record, one clears a 128-entry table, and one is a jump-only forwarder.
  • Verified Two checker limits were mapped to their exact causes in the checker sources. Scripted 64-bit callee answers wider than a signed 64-bit integer are rejected, plain script numbers always produce a zero high half, dictionary forms carrying a high half are zeroed before they reach the test process, and the per-call sequence form restarts every trial, so the high half of a 64-bit answer cannot currently be varied across trials.
  • Verified A store-order wrong version of one function passed repeatedly while an omit-the-stores version of the same function was caught at once, and a return-value canary proved fresh code was running. The cause is unknown.

What was decided or recommended

All twenty rewrites ship as verified with the narrowing stated in each result record. Later lanes with 64-bit callee answers should not rely on scripted high halves until the checker gap above is fixed, and should treat a passing reorder mutant as no evidence that stores are covered. The unexplained passing reorder mutant is recorded in the lane report for the checker owners.

How to reproduce it

Generate the crate, contracts and rewrites from the lane generator script, build the rewrite crate into the lane build folder, run the lane copy of the checker driver once per contract, and rebuild the lane results file from the verdicts; every verdict must pass with no vacuous flag and every wrong version must fail.

What was confusing or went wrong

Hand-counted call locations were wrong for eight of the twenty functions because data bytes can mimic call opcodes; a byte scan cross-checked with a disassembler fixed all of them, and a wrong location fails loudly at setup. One function's declared memory range came out slightly short and the checker reported it as writes outside the declared range on both sides, which pointed straight at the arithmetic slip. Trial speed varied more than tenfold over the session for no visible reason, so per-function timings in the results come from the verdict records, not from memory.

entry.title: Naming ranked episodic race leaderboard methods, boards 37 to 54
entry.summary: All 150 functions in this batch are per-board virtual methods of the ranked episodic race leaderboard descriptors, and every one is named with the same nine-method vocabulary earlier lanes established for this family.
entry.content:
All 150 functions in this batch are per-board virtual methods of the ranked episodic race leaderboard descriptors, and every one is named with the same nine-method vocabulary earlier lanes established for this family.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, which mostly come from the same source files, giving each a confidence of high, medium or low.

What was found

Verified The batch holds nine virtual methods for each of eighteen leaderboard boards, covering ranked episodic race boards 37 through 54. Two boards at the batch edges are partial, and two boards have no per-board id getter because their tables point into the encrypted region instead. Every method slot has exactly one code shape across all boards, and all boards agree internally on a single numeric board id.

Verified The nine methods per board are: a board-name getter, a board-id getter, a column-index search, a column-id lookup, a column-size lookup, a column-kind lookup, a mapped-column-index lookup, a column-id mapper, and a row builder that fills nineteen column positions plus a presence bitmask. The row-builder loop bound of nineteen matches the value measured for earlier boards of the same sub-family.

Verified Board ids are scattered rather than sequential: neighbouring race numbers can have far-apart ids, so later work must read each id from the code and never compute it from the race number.

What was decided or recommended

All 150 functions are named in the inherited vocabulary, 31 at high confidence and 119 at medium, with none left empty. The subsystem for the whole batch is online leaderboards. The next lane on this family should continue with the boards above race 54 using the same nine names, and keep checking id unanimity per board to catch anomalies mechanically.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the batch through the executable's memory-mapped image, group functions by code shape, and confirm each group matches one of the nine known slots. Attribute unlabelled entries through their virtual tables: a name getter is proven by the board-name string it returns, and a kind lookup by sitting at the expected table offset with its board's id constant. Cross-check that every method of one board carries the same id.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified Six id getters are referenced from foreign tables as well as their own, and two column-id lookups have extra raw matches inside bulk data whose neighbours are not code addresses at all. Both are known traps in this family: the first is linker-folded identical stubs, the second coincidental byte matches. Checking each reference's neighbours before counting it avoided both.

entry.title: Naming a block of leaderboard helpers, and a data-read trap
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive functions turned out to be nine virtual methods repeated across seventeen leaderboard types, and all of them could be named with high confidence. The same work caught a silent misread bug that made good name pointers look like garbage.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive functions turned out to be nine virtual methods repeated across seventeen leaderboard types, and all of them could be named with high confidence. The same work caught a silent misread bug that made good name pointers look like garbage.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a batch of one hundred fifty unnamed game functions that sit next to each other in the executable, working out what the group is about first and then naming each function.

What was found

Verified The batch holds nine virtual methods of seventeen leaderboard-info template types, one per ranked episodic board. Every method shape repeats exactly across all boards, differing only in a per-board numeric id.

Verified The nine methods are: a name getter returning the board's own full leaderboard name, an id getter returning the numeric board id, an index lookup that scans the id array, a row lookup by index, a column-width query, an entry-kind query, a reverse row search, a value-by-id lookup, and a row packer that loops over twenty-five columns classifying and copying values with a presence bitmask. Earlier verified rewrites of the same slots in other boards confirm seven of the nine behaviours, and the row packer was read in full.

Verified Thirty functions the inventory had no name for were identified by position and shape: sixteen six-byte name getters and fourteen entry-kind queries. A recovered vtable for one board lists them in exactly the expected slots.

Verified Tiny six-byte getters are shared across unrelated classes by the linker, so a vtable edge into such a small function does not prove which class it belongs to. Class attribution came from code position and the returned constant instead.

What was decided or recommended

All one hundred fifty functions were named in the established class-and-method style, reusing the wording earlier lanes agreed on for the same slots, since that wording matches the verified behaviour in every case. The next naming lane covering nearby boards can reuse the same nine-way slot map directly.

  • Check tiny shared functions by position and constant, not by vtable edges alone.
  • When reading data bytes through the memory-mapped image, index it by address minus image base. Never index it with a file offset.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble one function per slot with capstone through the section-data reader and compare mnemonic shapes across the batch. Resolve each direct call against the import table, the verified-rewrite index and earlier lane names. Read each name getter's target as a string and each id getter's immediate, then assert that every slot of one board shares one id. Recover one board's vtable by searching the image for a pointer to a known method and reading the surrounding pointers.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified Halfway through, every name pointer appeared to aim into the middle of unrelated strings, which made the name getter look like anything but a name getter. The cause was my own bug: the memory-mapped image buffer is indexed by address, and I had indexed it with file offsets, silently shifting every data read. Code reads were unaffected because they went through the section-data reader. Re-reading with correct indexing showed every pointer aims exactly at its own board's full name. The wrong readings were discarded and nothing in the final names depends on them.

entry.title: One replay-memory gate verified, and what its proof taught
entry.summary: A per-frame gate in the replay-memory block family passed the full differential proof, and the failures along the way exposed a silent contract trap, a dead computation in the original, and a rule for registers carried across intercepted calls.
entry.content:
A per-frame gate in the replay-memory block family passed the full differential proof, and the failures along the way exposed a silent contract trap, a dead computation in the original, and a rule for registers carried across intercepted calls.

What was asked

Rewrite three neighbouring mid-size functions from the files-memory subsystem in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original under the version 4 checker, with a deliberately wrong version run against every proof.

What was found

Verified The smallest of the three, a 369-byte gate with eleven direct calls and one tail jump, passed 1200 of 1200 trials with every check on, and the wrong version failed exactly on the heap as designed.

Verified That gate computes two scaled floats but only ever exposes the first: the range check reads the first product's spill slot while the second product is spilled to a slot nothing reads back. The proof covers every observable behaviour; the dead computation is documented, not hidden.

Verified Global addresses in proof contracts must be written as offsets from the image base, not as full addresses. The full form plants values silently at the wrong place, and every trial then fails the same way a null table would. A five-byte getter and a planted constant confirmed the diagnosis both ways.

Verified A callee that pops fewer words than were pushed is not a mismatch: the extra pushed word was the caller's saved register, which the callee never reads. Its real return cleanup, read from its own epilogue, settled the argument count when push-counting gave the wrong answer.

Inferred The two larger siblings belong to the same family and should verify with the same contract patterns; a complete unprobed contract, rewrite draft, and ordered probe checklist for the middle one is staged for the next lane.

What was decided or recommended

  • Mirror register threading exactly: the original reloads the object register with a selected factor between two poll calls, so the rewrite passes the factor, not the object.
  • Use the stub preserve flag only where the real callee provably preserves the register; skip the comparison with a note where the real body provably ignores it.
  • Pin float operation order from the start and write unordered-aware forms for every float comparison, including threshold tests.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contract generator for the small gate, build the lane crate for the 32-bit target into the lane build folder, and run the driver copy with 1200 trials on the stock worker; then run the bundled wrong version, which must fail on the heap comparison. The staged middle function needs its plan's probe checklist worked first.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first hour looked like the original was at fault: most trials faulted on both sides at once. Two of the causes were mine, a wrong address form and a wrong argument count, and both announced themselves as wild control transfers rather than clean mismatches. The mapping between file offsets and in-memory addresses also bit once at triage time and produced phantom calls until corrected.

entry.title: An aim routine that never returns on a zero offset
entry.summary: One input-ui routine loops forever when its two-dimensional offset is exactly zero, so rewrite proofs must exclude that input by construction; the same lane also learned that a probe passing only on shallow paths proves nothing about deep code.
entry.content:
One input-ui routine loops forever when its two-dimensional offset is exactly zero, so rewrite proofs must exclude that input by construction; the same lane also learned that a probe passing only on shallow paths proves nothing about deep code.

What was asked

Rewrite two neighbouring input-ui functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original over at least one thousand checker trials, with bit-exact float comparison and a deliberately wrong version that must fail.

What was found

Verified The smaller routine, an aim-angle clamp of about six hundred bytes, hangs the original when both components of its computed offset are zero: the magnitude becomes infinite and the angle wrapping loops never terminate. Fixed disjoint value sets for the matrix inputs and the callee outputs keep every trial away from zero, confirmed by a scripted check over all generated trials.

Verified The larger routine, a candidate-pair matcher of about three thousand bytes with fifteen callees, verified on the first attempt. Its proof observes all four computed matrix buffers through call snapshots; ten further words that are verbatim copies of scripted callee answers sit beyond the per-callee snapshot budget and are disclosed as unobserved.

Verified The first rewrite of the smaller routine had two wrapping loops inverted, hanging the rewrite on every trial that reached them, while all twenty-six passing probe trials exited early and never reached the loops. The pass count looked healthy; only the branch-shape count showed the deep code was never exercised.

What was decided or recommended

Both functions verified with the zero-offset input excluded by design and documented, since it hangs the original too. Lanes proving loop-heavy routines should check branch shapes on every probe run, not just the pass count, and should re-derive each loop condition from its exit jump rather than from the entry comparison.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane contract for the aim routine with matrix and callee-output pins drawn from overlapping value sets: trials where the offset comes out as exactly zero hit the trial watchdog on both sides identically. Replace either set with a disjoint one and all trials complete.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two full verification runs sat silent for over forty minutes with no verdict, which first looked like machine overload (more than twenty checker workers were running). A small sixty-trial probe finished quickly and pointed at the inverted loops instead; with the fix, the full run passed in under four minutes. The lesson held twice: small probes diagnose faster than staring at a silent full run.

entry.title: The memory shortage was one forgotten script
entry.summary: For most of a morning the lane count was held down by a shortage of memory that the coordinator put down to the number of lanes and to other programs on the machine. The real cause was one helper script, written by a lane that had finished four hours earlier, still running and holding 8.7 GB. Nine more leftover scripts were each spinning a processor core, some for thirteen hours. Stopping the ten of them took commit headroom from 12 GB to more than 21 and roughly halved processor load.
entry.content:
For most of a morning the lane count was held down by a shortage of memory that the coordinator put down to the number of lanes and to other programs on the machine. The real cause was one helper script, written by a lane that had finished four hours earlier, still running and holding 8.7 GB. Nine more leftover scripts were each spinning a processor core, some for thirteen hours. Stopping the ten of them took commit headroom from 12 GB to more than 21 and roughly halved processor load.

What was asked

Why only 26 lanes fitted when 45 had fitted the night before on the same machine with similar headroom.

What was found

FactValueWhat it means
Largest leftoverone script, 8.7 GB, four hours oldWritten by a large-function lane to simulate a stack; the lane finished, the script did not
Other leftoversnine scripts, small in memory, each using a full processor coreLoops that never ended; the oldest had run for almost fourteen hours

Verified The processes were found by walking each project process's ancestors: a lane's processes have a live agent above them, the coordinator's have its own program above them, and these had neither.

Verified The tick's watchdog did not catch the large one because it matched on script names used by the checker. The script had a different name.

What was decided or recommended

  • The watchdog now stops any of the project's script processes above 4 GB whatever it is called, and any left by a lane that is no longer running once it is two and a half hours old. It runs on every five-minute tick.
  • A health check runs with every hourly review: leftover and oversized processes, processes that will not exit, memory, commit, page file, disk, the supervisor, the repository. It is now part of the review rule.
  • Only the project's own processes are stopped. Other programs on the machine are reported.

How to reproduce it

List the script and checker processes whose command line points into the project's scratch folders, with their age, memory and processor time; mark each by whether the lane named in its path still has a live agent.

What was confusing or went wrong

The coordinator explained the shortage three times before finding it: first by lane count, then by wrapper processes, then by the owner's other programs, and asked him to close some. Each explanation fitted the totals by process name, because a table grouped by name shows one large group called "python" and nothing says that one member of it is most of the group. The number that should have prompted a closer look was available all along: 26 lanes did not fit where 45 had.

entry.title: Production batch blocked: task-system code span reads encrypted
entry.summary: A production batch of twenty small task-system functions could not be verified because the checker's worker faults on every trial: the code span reads as encrypted bytes through every independent reader, while the project inventory describes valid functions at the same locations.
entry.content:
A production batch of twenty small task-system functions could not be verified because the checker's worker faults on every trial: the code span reads as encrypted bytes through every independent reader, while the project inventory describes valid functions at the same locations.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty small neighbouring functions from the task subsystem in Rust and prove each rewrite equivalent to the original with the checker, deferring with a stated reason where the checker cannot verify.

What was found

Verified The worker faults on the original side of every trial, deterministically, with zero completed original trials, so no verdict could pass. Seventeen rewrites with contracts and one mutant each were completed and banked for re-run; three larger functions were triaged only.

Verified The batch span reads as random-looking bytes through the worker, direct file reads, and repeated hash checks, while other regions of the same file read as normal code and the stock regression passes.

Verified The repaired function inventory matches the banked rewrites exactly on all twenty entries: sizes, instruction counts and callee counts all agree, including shared jump tails and trap jumps. The inventory therefore describes the true code, and the current file bytes in this span do not.

Verified A small set of the lane's own early scripts decoded valid code from this span that matches the inventory exactly, while all other readers saw random bytes from the same path in the same minutes. A long series of controls (identical interpreters, libraries, paths and slices; swapped script contents; fresh nonces proving live execution; stable hashes) failed to find a natural mechanism, and the anomaly is unresolved.

What was decided or recommended

All seventeen completed functions were deferred as needing encrypted code, with rewrites and contracts kept for an unchanged re-run once decrypted bytes are available. Nothing is reported as verified. The coordinator was asked to establish why this span differs from the inventory ground truth, to audit writes to the original file, and to consider having the worker report a hash of its mapped image in every run.

How to reproduce it

Run any of this lane's banked contracts with the stock worker and observe every trial fault on the original side with no completed original trials. Compare the inventory's sizes and instruction counts for the batch against the banked rewrites. Read the lane report in the scratch area for the full control sequence behind the read anomaly.

What was confusing or went wrong

Most of the lane went to the read anomaly: two groups of scripts reading the same file path disagreed about its bytes with perfect script-correlation across dozens of runs, surviving every control that should have distinguished them. The lane stopped investigating at the time box with the mechanism unknown. The practical conclusion does not depend on it: the worker faults, so verification is impossible until the byte mismatch is resolved.

entry.title: Two silent proof-weakeners in production float work, and one deferred function
entry.summary: A production batch of three camera-math functions verified two and deferred one, but the durable result is two traps that silently weaken other lanes' proofs: combining two global-fill contract keys drops the random fill without warning, and the optimizing backend changes NaN payloads despite operand pinning. Both are now documented with workarounds.
entry.content:
A production batch of three camera-math functions verified two and deferred one, but the durable result is two traps that silently weaken other lanes' proofs: combining two global-fill contract keys drops the random fill without warning, and the optimizing backend changes NaN payloads despite operand pinning. Both are now documented with workarounds.

What was asked

Rewrite three adjacent medium-sized functions from the input-ui subsystem in Rust and prove each bit-identical to the original over at least one thousand trials, with one deliberately wrong version per function that must fail.

What was found

  • Verified Two leaf functions verified: one with four pointer arguments and no globals, one with no arguments and only globals, each one thousand out of one thousand trials bit-exact, each shipped wrong version caught, plus extra wrong versions proving every branch direction fires and is observed.
  • Verified The third function (five outgoing calls, three into encrypted code) is deferred: the lane's own translator lacks join-merges for registers assigned inside branches, so one branch path computes a stale value. The failure was traced to a single snapshot word; the fix design and a complete retry kit are in the lane folder.
  • Verified Contract trap: when a contract contains both a global fill mode and explicit global values, the driver returns early and the fill mode is silently ignored, so every unpinned global word is zero instead of random. Zero-masked computations then pass one thousand trials while hiding real bugs. The fix is to spell every word of every declared range explicitly.
  • Verified Codegen trap: identical rewrite source passes sixty out of sixty unoptimized and fails six out of sixty optimized, with NaN-payload-only differences. Operand pinning does not constrain the backend's operand choice, and explicit vector intrinsics did not help either. The shipped proofs use unoptimized builds.
  • Verified A nested call reads a stack leftover (the previous call's return address) through overlapping frames; three resulting global writes are deterministic in the harness but unobservable to any rewrite, so they are excluded from comparison and disclosed.

What was decided or recommended

  • Audit every existing contract that combines both global-fill keys: those proofs ran on zeros, not random fills, wherever words were unpinned. The driver should overlay the two or reject the combination.
  • Treat optimization level as load-bearing for float proofs: a bit-exact proof holds for the binary that ran, and re-optimizing can invalidate NaN behavior. Note the level in the contract record.
  • Single-pass translators must merge registers at branch joins; hoisting temporaries preserves scope but silently keeps one path's value. The deferred function is the concrete test case.

How to reproduce it

For the fill trap: write a contract with both a random global fill and one explicit global value, run a handful of trials, and dump the trial requests: unpinned words are pristine, not random. For the codegen trap: build any NaN-sensitive rewrite at two optimization levels from identical source and run the same float-edge contract against both; the optimized binary fails NaN-payload comparisons the unoptimized one passes.

What was confusing or went wrong

The zero-masked fills cost the most time: a one-thousand-trial pass looked conclusive until a narrowed-contract experiment showed a dropped store going unnoticed, which led back through several wrong theories (comparison limits, dead stores) to the driver's early return. The NaN failures were also misattributed twice (first to translation order, then to instruction selection) before an optimized-versus-unoptimized build of identical source isolated the backend. Both episodes argue for distrusting green runs that cannot produce a failing wrong version.

entry.title: A green verdict can still miss whole paths
entry.summary: A production batch of twenty small task-system functions verified at twenty out of twenty, each over one thousand trials with its deliberately wrong version caught, and a follow-up audit still found seven contracts that never ran some of their paths. The cause was period lock-in between callee scripts, and the fix was re-perioding, not rewriting.
entry.content:
A production batch of twenty small task-system functions verified at twenty out of twenty, each over one thousand trials with its deliberately wrong version caught, and a follow-up audit still found seven contracts that never ran some of their paths. The cause was period lock-in between callee scripts, and the fix was re-perioding, not rewriting.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty small game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite equivalent to the original with the checker, one contract and one wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified After the first full pass showed twenty greens with every declared callee firing, a branch-shape audit showed missing call sequences on seven contracts: null-detail paths, null-state paths, and second-answer values that never appeared on firing trials. In each case a callee answer script shared its cycle length with the gate that decides whether the callee runs, so the gate outcome and the answer locked together and some combinations never occurred in any trial count.

Verified Re-perioding the scripts to lengths three, five and seven, with residues tabulated by hand so every value fires where it matters, restored the missing shapes (one contract went from eight distinct call sequences to ten) and all re-runs passed with their wrong versions still caught. No rewrite changed in this round.

Verified One function's early exits clear only the low byte of the result register, leaving input-determined upper bytes; the rewrite reproduces them exactly and the comparison covers the full register. Five step functions call through object function tables; planting the harness stubs in fabricated tables verified all of them with no skipped or masked arguments.

What was decided or recommended

Every contract with a gated callee should have its script periods checked against the gate's period before the full run: equal periods with aligned phases lock. After the run, the distinct call-sequence shapes should be compared against the paths read from the disassembly, not just counted. A wrong version that only touches an observed path cannot catch this; the audit is the control.

How to reproduce it

Take any contract where a callee answer cycles with period two behind a gate that also varies with period two, run it, and list the distinct call sequences in the verdict: one expected short shape will be absent. Change the script to period three and re-run: the shape appears.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first triage decoded garbage because the script indexed the mapped image by file offset instead of address; the brief's mapping warning caught it. A push of a register that looked like a sixth call argument turned out to be stack allocation for a float slot, found when the original faulted on every trial. The rewrite library could not be deleted after checker runs even though no process held it as a loaded module; renaming it aside before each build worked around it. Piping a running checker into a truncating pager once killed the driver silently mid-run, losing a wrong-version run; all full runs redirect to log files.

entry.title: Where a checker trial's time goes
entry.summary: Most of a checker trial's wall time was spent waiting for a newly created worker thread to run for the first time, not in the trial itself or in the driver. Reusing one worker thread across trials roughly doubled checker throughput with identical verdicts.
entry.content:
Most of a checker trial's wall time was spent waiting for a newly created worker thread to run for the first time, not in the trial itself or in the driver. Reusing one worker thread across trials roughly doubled checker throughput with identical verdicts.

What was asked

Make checker runs faster without changing any verdict. Checker time was about half of a small-function lane's waiting time, so any saving applies to every lane at once.

What was found

Verified A profile of three contracts of different shapes (one tiny, one with large heap inputs, one with scripted callees and full-data comparison) showed every driver-side stage together costing under half a millisecond per trial: input generation, request encoding, pipe write, response decoding and bookkeeping. A bare pipe round trip measures three hundredths of a millisecond.

Verified The same profile showed the worker's round trip taking about fifty milliseconds per trial for the tiny contract while the worker's own account of the trial work was about twelve. Bracketing inside a scratch copy of the worker split the gap: parsing and preparing a trial take tens of microseconds, creating the per-trial thread takes about sixty microseconds, and then roughly forty-seven milliseconds pass before the new thread's first instruction runs. That lag is constant across contracts while the trial body varies from eighteen to over three hundred milliseconds.

Verified Replacing the per-trial thread with one persistent thread per worker process removed the lag. The full tracked suite runs in about eight hundred seconds instead of about seventeen hundred (about twenty-four trials per second instead of about eleven). All thirty-eight tracked verdicts and all thirty-four mutant verdicts reproduce field for field except timings; one run's retry record differed by a single load-caused entry and a rerun matched fully. Thirty-four lane contracts of varied shapes with their rewrites were compared the same way with the same outcome.

Verified What limits trials now is the trial work itself (both sides executed plus the worker's comparison loops) and scheduler wake latency for the worker thread on a saturated machine, measured at up to about twelve milliseconds per trial. The driver, encoding and pipe remain noise.

Stage of one tiny-function trialMedian cost beforeMedian cost after
Driver: inputs, encoding, pipe, decodingunder half a millisecondunchanged
New thread's first schedulingabout forty-seven millisecondspaid once per worker, hidden in setup
Trial work, both sides plus comparisonabout twelve millisecondsunchanged
Waking the reused threadnot presentzero to twelve milliseconds, load-driven

What was decided or recommended

  • Integrate the persistent trial thread: it is worker-internal, changes no protocol bytes, and keeps the hang behaviour (a timed-out trial still abandons the thread and the worker still exits for a fresh one).
  • Do not pursue batched requests, slimmer responses, or reworked encoding for speed: the stages they would improve sum to under half a millisecond.
  • Running one contract's trials across several workers in parallel is sound in principle (trials are seeded and independent, and results merge deterministically), but it needs a check that every worker mapped memory identically, and it only helps while processors are free. The machine already runs about twenty workers at full load, so pair it with a global worker cap. Not built.

How to reproduce it

Build the worker from the scratch copy in the lane folder, run the tracked suite twice with the stock driver (once per worker binary), and compare the two output folders field by field with the lane's comparison script, ignoring only the two timing fields. Then run the lane's contract runner over its selected contract list, which exercises both workers itself, and compare again. Exact commands are in the lane's change notes.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The starting assumption pointed at the driver and the pipe; the first profile disproved it within minutes. Absolute times swing severalfold with machine load, so only back-to-back pairs are quoted. A first attempt at scanning every lane contract file ran too long and was replaced by checking the cheap filter (a rewrite binary on disk) before parsing. Rebuilding the worker twice into one folder once failed with an access error while no process held the file, so the scratch binary was built under a distinct name.

What was asked

Build the project's function ledger: one database with one row per function, an importer that ingests today's scattered sources, proof that it reproduces the current counts and queue, the queries the coordinator needs, and a migration plan that keeps the five-minute loop working throughout.

Verified The earlier review's three drifts reproduce: hundreds of rewrites carry a recorded checker version older than the verdict on disk, tens of verdicts match no contract on file, and the named count feeds through a file only one script writes.

Verified Fifteen disagreements between the scripts themselves, the largest being finished lanes whose aggregate-only result files both counting scripts skip silently, batches held forever by finished lanes, pilot batches that block the production queue permanently, and an hourly review that uses a different function universe than the site.

The query tool answers counts, batches, stale proofs, defer reasons, lane durations and brief rates.

The machine never sits still: five of six parity runs were interrupted by real concurrent writes, each traced to a named file. A batch-size parameter was shadowed by a loop variable and returned short batches until fixed. entry.title: One batch, two stack surprises: a shared argument slot and reads from unwritten stack
entry.summary: Verifying twenty small task-system functions turned up two stack behaviors worth knowing: one function passes a single pushed word to two calls in a row, and another reads its interpolation factor and one output word from stack slots it never wrote. The first is fully verified; the second made its function unverifiable and it was deferred.
entry.content:
Verifying twenty small task-system functions turned up two stack behaviors worth knowing: one function passes a single pushed word to two calls in a row, and another reads its interpolation factor and one output word from stack slots it never wrote. The first is fully verified; the second made its function unverifiable and it was deferred.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty small game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the checker, one function at a time, with a deliberately wrong version per function to show the contract can tell right from wrong.

What was found

Verified A record-kind check function pushes one word, makes an indirect call through an object table, then makes a direct call documented to pop one word. Stack-balance analysis plus the checker's fault report show the indirect callee pops nothing: both calls share the one pushed slot, and the direct callee consumes it. Declaring the indirect callee as taking register and stack arguments without popping (the checker's no-cleanup option) passes one thousand trials with full argument comparison.

Verified Two sibling index state machines return a constant that looks like dead initialization on two of their exit paths. The constant is set once at entry and two paths reach the shared epilogue without overwriting it. Wrong versions returning the plausible constants fail, confirming the behavior and the coverage.

Inferred A route-point interpolation function stores its call result four bytes below where it reloads the factor it multiplies with, and reads one output word sixteen bytes past the value it resembles. Both reads land on uninitialized frame space and caller stack, so the outputs depend on stack garbage and entry alignment rather than on the inputs. This was read from the disassembly three times, including the raw store and reload offsets, but not confirmed by running.

What was decided or recommended

  • Verifying nineteen of twenty, deferring the interpolation function with reason other and the analysis above, rather than shipping a rewrite fitted to the harness fills.
  • When a push sits before an indirect call with no stack cleanup after it, prove which call consumes the slot before declaring conventions; the no-cleanup stub option works for table-planted calls too.
  • Simulate pin and script periods as trial-index arithmetic in the contract generator and assert every path is hit; this caught four silent coverage locks before any trials ran.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the batch's functions from the executable with capstone through the mapped image, check each call site's pushes against the callee's stack cleanup, and compare the store and reload offsets of every spilled float. The coverage models live in the lane's contract generator scripts.

What was confusing or went wrong

The shared-slot function first presented as a checker defect: the original faulted at the pushed heap address on every trial while the rewrite passed. Tracing the stack word by word showed the contract was wrong, not the worker: my declaration made the stub pop a word the real callee leaves. A second function failed on eight trials with the original returning a heap address where zero was expected; the early exit clears the low byte of an address register that still holds the probe pointer, not the flag word that was only compared. Both fixes were one line each.
