entry.title: A view-system initializer that reads its own uninitialized stack
entry.summary: One of this week's production functions stores a word it never wrote to sixteen globals, so its behaviour is whatever the stack happened to hold. The rewrite reproduces the read itself under a pinned zero fill, and all seven functions in the batch verified.
entry.content:
One of this week's production functions stores a word it never wrote to sixteen globals, so its behaviour is whatever the stack happened to hold. The rewrite reproduces the read itself under a pinned zero fill, and all seven functions in the batch verified.

What was asked

Rewrite seven neighbouring view-system functions in Rust and prove each one equal to the original with the differential checker: a record copier, two row rebuilders, a frustum updater, a target recreator, a target releaser and a system initializer.

What was found

  • Verified All seven verified at twelve hundred trials each with no failures, and all seven deliberately wrong versions were caught.
  • Verified The initializer reads one word from a part of its stack frame it never wrote, then stores that word to sixteen global slots. Address arithmetic on its prologue shows the read always lands in the unwritten area, so in the game the value is leftover stack garbage and differs from run to run.
  • Verified The two row rebuilders are twins that differ by a single instruction: one scales by a stored word, the other by zero.
  • Verified Three values one twin computes only ever reach stack slots that are overwritten before any read, so the rewrite omits them with no observable difference.

What was decided or recommended

The rewrite performs the same uninitialized read on its own stack slot, and the proof pins the checker's stack fill to zero so both sides deterministically read zero. The proof is therefore conditional on that fill, and it is recorded as such. Recommendation for other lanes: when a function spills to its incoming argument slot or reads scratch it did not write, check the frame arithmetic before assuming the contract is wrong.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contracts for the batch with the stock worker; the initializer's contract sets a zero stack fill, and its rewrite reads an uninitialized local through a volatile load as its first act. Changing the fill or zeroing the slot in the rewrite breaks the match, which shows the read is real.

What was confusing or went wrong

The main rewrite library stayed locked for eleven minutes after a checker run with no holder found among the worker processes, so the last function was built in a second small crate in the same build folder. An early attempt at the releaser called through one level of indirection too few, which a single-trial debug trace showed as the original jumping to garbage while the rewrite passed. A first attempt at the initializer returned a loop variable instead of the stubbed callee's answer.

entry.title: Three ways the coordinator lost lanes in one morning
entry.summary: Twelve experiment lanes were reported as launched and never ran; eight production lanes were killed by a restart of the supervisor; and the lane assembling the rewrites into a loadable library was stopped at the two-hour limit with nothing written down. All three come from the same gap: the coordinator did not know what happens to a lane's process when the thing that started it ends. That is now tested and written into the operating notes.
entry.content:
Twelve experiment lanes were reported as launched and never ran; eight production lanes were killed by a restart of the supervisor; and the lane assembling the rewrites into a loadable library was stopped at the two-hour limit with nothing written down. All three come from the same gap: the coordinator did not know what happens to a lane's process when the thing that started it ends. That is now tested and written into the operating notes.

What was asked

Why experiment lanes had no log files half an hour after their launch was announced, and why nine lanes showed an error exit in the hourly review.

What was found

How the launcher endedWhat happened to its lanesHow it is known
Stopped by handKilled with it. Eight lanes died in the same second.Their logs all end at the moment the supervisor was stopped to change a setting.
Stopped by the two-hour limit on background tasksKilled with it. The assembly lane lost two hours of work; several lanes started by slots went the same way earlier and had been counted only as "not running".The lane's log ends within the minute of the limit; no agent process remained.
Ended normallyThey keep running.A test launcher started a child, exited after eight seconds, and the child kept writing for as long as it was watched.
A short foreground command that starts detached processes and returnsNothing started at all: no log line, no output, no process.Twelve lanes prepared this way had no log file thirty minutes later.

Verified Each row was observed today. The earlier note in this log's operating entry, that a lane outlives its launcher when the launcher is stopped, was wrong; it holds only when the launcher ends normally.

Unknown Why detached processes started from a foreground command did not run. It was not investigated further once a working method existed.

What was decided or recommended

  • Lanes are started only from a long-lived background launcher, which ends by itself before the two-hour limit and is never stopped by hand. Its settings are changed through a file it reads on every pass.
  • A launch is not reported until the lane's log file exists.
  • A lane started directly as its own background task is told to write its results file in the first minutes and keep it current, and to finish well inside two hours. The assembly lane was restarted with that instruction and an 80-minute budget.
  • A lane that dies without results gives its batch back to the queue on the next tick, but never within fifteen minutes of its launch.

How to reproduce it

Start a launcher that starts a child writing a heartbeat line every five seconds. End the launcher three ways (let it finish, stop it, let it hit the time limit) and watch whether the heartbeat continues.

What was confusing or went wrong

The coordinator announced the experiment lanes from the launch script's own output, which printed the lane names it had prepared. Printing a name is not evidence that a process is running. The half hour was lost because the check that would have shown it, whether each lane had a log file, was run only when results were expected.

entry.title: Black box does not pin down float multiply order
entry.summary: Verified Wrapping one operand of a float multiply in a compiler black box does not stop the compiler backend from swapping the operands, so a rewrite can still pick the wrong NaN payload. Selecting NaN operands explicitly in plain code fixes it reliably.
entry.content:
Verified Wrapping one operand of a float multiply in a compiler black box does not stop the compiler backend from swapping the operands, so a rewrite can still pick the wrong NaN payload. Selecting NaN operands explicitly in plain code fixes it reliably.

What was asked

One function in this production batch multiplies two single-precision values and returns the product through the floating point register. One trial in a thousand failed with only NaN sign and payload bits differing, which points at swapped multiply operands: with two different NaNs, the hardware keeps the destination operand's NaN, so operand order is observable.

What was found

Verified The project guidance for this case is to write the operations in the original order and keep the compiler from commuting them with a black box on one operand. That changed nothing: the same seeded trial failed with bit-identical wrong output before and after.

Verified Disassembling the freshly built rewrite showed why. Both multiplies in the function had been emitted with the operands exchanged relative to the source: the value written first in the source ended up as the source operand instead of the destination. The black box only constrains an earlier compiler stage; the later backend pass that assigns the destination register commutes freely either way.

Verified Replaying that trial's inputs by hand confirmed the mechanism exactly: the original returns the destination NaN and the swapped rewrite returns the source NaN. After replacing each multiply and add with an explicit selection (destination NaN wins, else source NaN, else the plain operation, all in ordinary code with no assembly), the same seeded trial passes along with the other 999.

What was decided or recommended

Rewrites in this lane select NaN operands explicitly wherever both inputs of a multiply or add can be NaN. Subtract, divide, compare and negate cannot be commuted and stay plain. Any lane relying on a black box for operand order should re-check: a passing verdict whose trials never combined two different NaNs proves nothing about order, and the build can differ from the source silently.

How to reproduce it

Take a function whose result is a multiply of two f32 values that can both be NaN with different payloads. Write the multiply in the original order with one operand through a black box, build the rewrite, and disassemble the built export: the emitted multiply may list the operands exchanged. Then run a trial with two different NaN inputs and compare the result bits against the original.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first diagnosis looked like an ordinary operand-order slip in the rewrite, and the prescribed one-line fix compiled cleanly, so the identical second failure was genuinely surprising. What unblocked it was stopping trusting the source text and reading the built machine code instead. A second, smaller trap in the same lane: two scratch memory segments overlapped by eight bytes, so random words silently overwrote a pinned value and every trial faulted; the driver does not check for overlap.

A production batch of twenty small game functions verified eighteen of them, and three of the eighteen only mismatch the original in stack or stack-pointer bookkeeping that no safe rewrite can reproduce; the values themselves match through other checks.

What was asked

Rewrite twenty neighbouring game functions from the pedestrian and task subsystem in Rust and prove each one equivalent to the original with the differential checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares return values, memory, stack behaviour, calls and faults.

What was found

Verified Eighteen functions passed one thousand trials each with no failures, including two that call through fabricated object tables and one with a computed tail jump. Two functions were deferred with stated reasons.

What was decided or recommended

Disabling a single bookkeeping comparison is acceptable when a prior full run shows everything else green, the difference is a proven interception artifact rather than behaviour, and the values are verified through another comparison; the verdict and contract keep this visible for review. Lanes hitting a locked rewrite library should rename it aside and rebuild rather than stopping shared workers. The two deferred functions go back to the queue with their blocker codes.

How to reproduce it

Build the lane rewrite crate for 32-bit Windows with panics set to abort, then run the lane driver copy once per contract with the stock worker binary; each contract pins branch coverage with per-trial value cycles and runs one thousand trials. The lane folder keeps the contracts, verdicts, single-function rewrite files, generation scripts and the mutant probe.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two branch misreads on one function each failed half the trials: a below-threshold jump returns the source point rather than falling through, and a null link still takes the measuring path. One rewrite passed raw image addresses where relocated ones were needed, which the call detail exposed as unnormalised values. One verdict ran against a stale library after a locked rebuild; the file timestamp caught it and the run was repeated.

entry.title: The optimizer can silently change NaN results
entry.summary: A rewrite that matched the original on 1099 of 1100 trials failed the last one only because the compiler had packed three independent float computations into vector instructions, swapping the operands of one addition. Where no NaN is involved the swap is harmless, which is why it passed 1099 times. The fix is to fence each computation so the optimizer keeps it scalar and in order.
entry.content:
A rewrite that matched the original on 1099 of 1100 trials failed the last one only because the compiler had packed three independent float computations into vector instructions, swapping the operands of one addition. Where no NaN is involved the swap is harmless, which is why it passed 1099 times. The fix is to fence each computation so the optimizer keeps it scalar and in order.

What was asked

Rewrite two input-handling functions in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares return values, memory, calls and faults bit for bit.

What was found

Verified Both functions verified, 1100 of 1100 trials each. The larger one transforms eight corners of a box and accumulates a bounding box, with heavy single-precision arithmetic and min/max merging that must match bit for bit, including NaN payloads.

Verified The single failure was a NaN payload mismatch: the original propagated an input NaN unchanged while the rewrite produced a canonical NaN. Disassembling the rewrite showed packed vector arithmetic where scalar operations were written. Restoring scalar order with optimization barriers fixed it, confirmed by checking the generated code contains no packed arithmetic.

Verified A separate coverage trap: when every contract input cycled with period two, all main-path trials took the same combination of branches, hiding the multi-call paths entirely. Mixing period-three and period-two cycles exposed them, and the newly covered paths immediately caught a real mistake in the rewrite.

What was decided or recommended

Float rewrites whose results must match bit for bit should fence independent rows or stages against vectorization and have their generated code checked for packed arithmetic, not just their source reviewed. Contracts should mix input cycle lengths and their branch-shape counts should be read, not just the pass or fail.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's checker contracts for the batch: the verdict files record 1100 passing trials each with full branch coverage. Reverting the barriers reproduces the single-trial NaN mismatch.

What was confusing or went wrong

The NaN failure was confusing at first because the source code had the operations in exactly the right order; the reordering happened invisibly at compile time. An earlier scare about empty disassembly turned out to be simple arithmetic: a size computed as a negative number, which the parsing library answers with empty bytes instead of an error.

entry.content:
Verified A further one hundred and fifty consecutive functions are the same nine leaderboard schema methods already named for the sibling board family, repeated once per standard racing leaderboard, and all one hundred and fifty are named with the same vocabulary. The new facts are that these boards pack five columns per row instead of seven, and that three boards keep their tiny id getter in the encrypted code region, folded together with unrelated classes.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first and then naming each function, with a confidence per name.

What was found

Verified The batch covers eighteen standard racing leaderboards with the same nine methods per board: a name getter, an id getter, column index, id, size and kind lookups, two cross-list mappers, and a row packing routine. Every copy of a method matches its siblings except for the board number constant. Thirty-two names are high confidence and one hundred and eighteen are medium.

Verified Checking each board's virtual table confirmed all thirty-two entries the inventory had left unattributed: the entries without vtable edges are genuine methods sitting in their expected slots, and the board each belongs to matches the attribution from code position, name string and board number in every case.

Verified Three boards have no readable id getter: their table slot points into the encrypted code region, at addresses also claimed by unrelated classes. The row builder loops over five columns here rather than the seven seen in the sibling family.

Inferred The three unreadable id getters are most likely identical six-byte constant loaders merged by the linker with other classes' getters, with the merged copies landing inside encrypted ranges; their ids are then the same small numbers the boards' other methods already pass around. A memory dump from the running game would settle it.

What was decided or recommended

  • Keep one shared vocabulary for this whole template family: the nine names from the earlier batch apply unchanged to every board, so future batches need verification only, not fresh naming.
  • Treat tiny constant-returning functions claimed by several unrelated classes as linker-folded copies, not inventory errors; the claim shared by the most plausible owner is usually still right.
  • A lane with a memory dump should read the three encrypted id getters and the shared schema helpers, which would confirm the remaining ids and the five column type codes.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble one copy of each distinct code shape through the mapped image, then confirm slot assignments by reading each board's virtual table starting from its name getter pointer: the entries after it identify the id getter and the column methods in order, including entries the inventory never attached.

What was confusing or went wrong

A scan for board number constants first reported two boards as having none, because the disassembler prints small values in decimal and the pattern only matched hexadecimal; widening it showed both boards pass small numbers consistently. The encrypted id getters briefly looked like a naming anomaly from an earlier batch until the table contents showed their methods and ids agree.

entry.summary: One hundred fifty leaderboard-info methods across seventeen race boards were named with an earlier batch's nine-method vocabulary after independent verification, and two assumptions from that earlier batch turned out not to hold everywhere.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty leaderboard-info methods across seventeen race boards were named with an earlier batch's nine-method vocabulary after independent verification, and two assumptions from that earlier batch turned out not to hold everywhere.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a consecutive run of unnamed game functions, all per-board virtual methods of the ranked-race leaderboard info template, covering seven no-holds race boards and ten standard race boards.

What was found

Verified All nine method skeletons from the earlier leaderboard batch recur exactly, one per virtual-table slot, differing only in a board-id number and name-string reference. Every function was disassembled and every instruction count matched the inventory's hints.

Verified Board ids are not a linear function of race number in this range. The standard boards run sequentially, but the no-holds boards have gaps, and two adjacent boards take ids in inverted order. All methods within each board agree on the id, so the assignment is real and the inversion is flagged, not a misread.

Verified Two board-id getter stubs are also referenced from unrelated animation-class tables, and spot checks show the sharing is genuine: each stub sits at the expected slot of its own board's table and returns the board's id, while the outside references sit in vtable-like pointer runs, one at exactly the attributed slot offset. The likely explanation is linker folding of identical constant-returning bytes.

What was decided or recommended

All one hundred fifty functions were named, thirty-four at high confidence and the rest at medium, with none left empty. Future naming work in this family should always read the board id from the code rather than computing it from the race number, and should treat outside-class attributions on six-byte id stubs as real sharing to be confirmed by own-table membership, not as inventory noise.

Disassemble each function through the executable's memory-mapped image, cluster by instruction skeleton, extract the small immediate each schema method passes to the shared helper and the constant each six-byte stub returns, read the referenced board-name strings, and confirm slot membership by locating each board's virtual table in read-only data.

What was confusing or went wrong

The two animation-class attributions first looked like inventory errors, since a leaderboard id getter has no business in an animation table. entry.title: Splitting the checker worker without changing it
entry.summary: The checker worker, previously one file of about three thousand lines, is now split into six modules plus the entry point, with its one global fenced by an explicit rule and forty new unit tests, and every proof of sameness passes: identical emitted bytes on all contracts and an identical full regression.
entry.content:
The checker worker, previously one file of about three thousand lines, is now split into six modules plus the entry point, with its one global fenced by an explicit rule and forty new unit tests, and every proof of sameness passes: identical emitted bytes on all contracts and an identical full regression.

What was asked

Split the worker file along component lines (protocol, state, image mapping, execution, call interception, trial orchestration) as a refactor only: no behaviour change, no new features, no renamed protocol fields. Quarantine the single global so only the operating-system boundary and the entry point touch it directly. Add tests that need no game file. Prove nothing changed with a byte dump and the full regression suite.

What was found

Verified The file held eighty top-level items, which sliced mechanically into the six planned modules; the entry point kept only the command loop.

Verified The global accessor had about forty call sites. Eight functions on the main thread now take the state as a parameter; thirty-one sites stay global, almost all because they run on the trial thread, which cannot receive state across the thread spawn without synchronization. Each kept site carries a comment saying why.

Verified Emitted bytes are identical before and after: a debug command re-emitting every call stub, tail stub and patch for each of the thirty-eight proof contracts produced zero differing entries across all three proof builds.

Verified The full regression is identical before and after: thirty-eight contracts, thirty-five passing with three failing by design, thirty-four mutants caught, zero differing verdict fields.

Verified Forty unit tests run on the host with no game file and all pass, covering the following areas:

AreaTestsWhat they check
Json parsing7Objects, nesting, escapes, number scaling, errors, helpers
Comparison21Pointer windows, every result channel, truncation and mask rules, accumulator rules, nan diagnostic
Scratch layout3No two tables overlap for any allowed log size
Stub emission2Golden bytes for eight synthetic callees, patch correctness
Image helpers4Endian readers, string conversion, import lookup on a synthetic tree
Execution helpers3Deterministic fills, hash accumulation, observation rendering

Verified No defect was found in the worker while moving the code. Two suspicious-looking spots were examined and are correct as written.

What was decided or recommended

The command loop stays in the entry point rather than moving to the protocol module, because the quarantine rule permits the global there and holding a state borrow across the trial-thread spawn would alias the trial thread's access. The one-side runner lives with the execution engine rather than the trial orchestration, keeping the unsafe core reviewable apart. The scratch-region offsets became named constants so the layout test is coupled to the code instead of duplicating numbers. The debug dump command exists only to prove the split and can be dropped on integration; either way one more regression run after integrating is recommended.

How to reproduce it

Build the worker for its 32-bit target, record the debug byte dump for every proof contract, run the full regression suite, then split, quarantine and re-run: the dump comparison and the run comparison must both report zero differences. Run the unit tests with the standard test command on the host; they need no game file. The exact commands are recorded with the lane's module map.

What was confusing or went wrong

The shell reported failed exit codes for successful builds because the toolchain writes progress to the error stream; results were judged by the output text instead. The shared test fixture holds a callee with a register transport, which the fail-closed validation requires to be selected in every comparison test, so the test contracts had to select it, mirroring real driver behaviour. Paths that execute machine code or touch mapped memory cannot be unit-tested on the host and stay covered by the dump and the regression instead.

entry.title: The inventory entries that were never fully confirmed
entry.summary: Most of the inventory entries that boundary repair could not fully confirm are real functions after all: 3,260 out of 3,661, about nine in ten. The rest split into 183 fragments of other functions, 138 data entries such as jump tables and padding, and 80 that stay unsure. Both naming lanes that had reported doubtful entries were vindicated, one of them only after a second, pattern-specific analysis proved the general method blind in its region.
entry.content:
Most of the inventory entries that boundary repair could not fully confirm are real functions after all: 3,260 out of 3,661, about nine in ten. The rest split into 183 fragments of other functions, 138 data entries such as jump tables and padding, and 80 that stay unsure. Both naming lanes that had reported doubtful entries were vindicated, one of them only after a second, pattern-specific analysis proved the general method blind in its region.

What was asked

Give a verdict on every game-code inventory entry whose repair class is weaker than fully confirmed: real function, fragment of another function, data, unreadable, or unsure. Calibrate the method against two thousand fully confirmed entries and every verified entry in the weaker classes, which must all come out as functions. Judge two naming lanes' claims of bogus entries independently, entry by entry. Scan the code the inventory does not cover for missing functions.

What was found

Verified The weaker classes are overwhelmingly real: all of the thunk and Ghidra-only classes came out as functions, and the size-corrected and weakly confirmed classes are nearly all functions too. Only the gapfill-invented enclosing starts are mostly bad, at about three quarters fragments or data.

Verified The first naming lane was right on all 33 of its claimed bogus entries: none is a routine start. Twenty-five start in the middle of a machine instruction and eight are aligned interior points of neighbouring factory routines. None appears in the pointer table that references every genuine routine in its region, while all 117 genuine ones do.

Verified The second naming lane was right on all 9 of its claimed data entries, and partly right about missing functions: one claimed function is genuinely missing, swallowed by an oversized neighbouring range, and a set of plausible stub series was found where it predicted lookups. Three of its claimed missing functions turned out to be correctly attributed bodies of jump relays, and one was already in the inventory.

Verified Calibration passed at 2,050 out of 2,052. The two mismatches are genuine exception-handling funclets sitting in the fully confirmed class, the same family an earlier lane had found elsewhere. No verified rewrite sits on a bad entry. Four bad entries reached production batches and about ninety reached naming batches.

Verified The uncovered-code scan lists about seventeen hundred code runs, of which 129 plausibly start functions, holding an estimated 383 nested functions once series of tiny stubs are counted individually. The factory region additionally hides about two hundred true routine starts that the inventory lacks, shadowed by the oversized ranges of the bogus entries.

What was decided or recommended

  • Remove or annotate the 321 fragment and data entries, starting with the few already handed to production and naming lanes.
  • Repair the factory region as one edit: drop the 33 bogus entries and add the missing true starts, instead of only removing.
  • Add the plausible missing runs and the confirmed shadowed function to the inventory.
  • Keep the remaining weaker-class entries in the work queue; the calibration supports them.
  • Re-run the verdict script once the encrypted part of the code is readable; the unsure entries and the funclets hiding in the confirmed class should resolve then.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's verdict script over the repaired inventory with the section-based address mapping, then the tiling analysis for the factory region, then the missing-code scan with jump-table-aware judging. The mapping was proved on three verified functions first, and the call-target count reproduces the published cross-check number exactly. All verdicts, reasons, and the missing-run list are stored as data files with the lane's outputs.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The first version of the method judged the first naming lane wrong on all 33 entries, because the factory region has no analysis coverage and the fallback checks accept any clean-looking decode. A backward test that counted decoding from the entry itself as confirmation made it worse. Only the tiling analysis, which decodes forward from true routine starts and watches the claimed entries fall inside, settled it. The lesson is that empty coverage needs pattern-specific tests, and that a method must be doubted as readily as a lane.

Verified The missing scan first reported over five hundred plausible runs, most of them jump tables that looked targeted because a relocation entry holding a table's own address was mistaken for a function pointer. Skipping table prefixes before judging fixed it. A mid-instruction decode often re-synchronises into plausible code within a few instructions, so a clean decode alone never confirms an entry.

entry.content:

Name each function in the batch from static evidence, with confidence levels, continuing the project's naming conventions.

entry.title: Four input-UI functions: three verified, and a checker blind spot found with mutants
entry.summary: Three of four functions in this batch were rewritten in Rust and accepted by the checker. The fourth passed its contract but was deferred, because a passing result there does not cover half of the data it builds. Two things about the original code and the checker are worth knowing before the next lane picks up similar functions.
entry.content:
Three of four functions in this batch were rewritten in Rust and accepted by the checker. The fourth passed its contract but was deferred, because a passing result there does not cover half of the data it builds. Two things about the original code and the checker are worth knowing before the next lane picks up similar functions.

What was asked

Rewrite four neighbouring functions of the input and interface subsystem (between 612 and 1,443 bytes each) in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves like the original, using the stock checker worker only. At least 1,000 trials per function.

What was found

Verified The four functions belong to one module that uploads effect constants: one initialises two record tables and a block of settings, two build constant vectors from a selected record, and one submits a textured rectangle through the getters of two objects. Three were checked with 1,200 of 1,200 trials, the call logs compared word by word, and 14 of 14 hand-made wrong versions (mutants) were caught.

Verified The initialiser stores two floating point values into every record of the first table that it never sets itself. They are leftover stack contents. With a defined zero fill of the stack the rewrite (which writes zero) matches; with a patterned fill every trial fails on the written globals, which confirms that the original reads uninitialised memory. The same is true of one unused word per matrix row in a fourth function. In the shipped game these values depend on whatever the stack held.

Verified The checker can see only the first 8 words behind a pointer argument that points into the function's own frame. The deferred function builds a 16-word matrix in its frame and hands its address to a callee, so only the first two rows are compared. Wrong versions that change the first rows fail (193 of 300 trials); wrong versions that change the third row or the translation row, which holds the most involved arithmetic, pass all 300 trials. A passing contract there is not evidence about those words.

FunctionOutcomeTrialsMutants caught
Table initialiser (913 bytes)verified1,200 of 1,2005 of 5
Slot constants upload (612 bytes)verified1,200 of 1,2006 of 6
Textured rectangle submit (650 bytes)verified1,200 of 1,200 and 1,200 of 1,200 with wide inputs3 of 3

What was decided or recommended

Inferred The deferred function should be finished by lifting the snapshot limit in the stock worker (more than 8 words, or a word offset from the pointer), not by a private worker. The stage-1 rewrite and contract are kept so the next lane only adds the missing snapshots. Until then no result for a function that passes frame buffers of more than 8 words to a callee should be counted as complete unless a mutant in the later words has been shown to fail.

Inferred Contracts for float code should use inputs in a range where small terms survive rounding. A first contract with wide random integers caught one wrong version in only 2 of 300 trials, because a half-texel offset vanishes next to a quotient in the millions; with moderate pixel values the same wrong version fails 221 of 300.

How to reproduce it

  1. Write the rewrites against the checker runtime and build them into the lane's own build folder.
  2. Describe each callee in the contract: calls through an object's table are answered by planted stubs, pointers into the function's own frame are skipped and replaced by a snapshot of the words behind them.
  3. Run the contract on the stock worker; then run hand-made wrong versions against the same contract and check that each fails, including versions that change the words you believe are compared.
  4. Repeat the initialiser's contract once with the patterned stack fill to see the uninitialised reads.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified Thiscall callees are compared on their object register by default, so a pointer into the function's own frame fails every trial until the contract lists no compared registers for that callee. This cost two attempts on the initialiser. Several callees live in the encrypted part of the code and cannot be read, so their stack clean-up was inferred from the callers; the passing stack checks support the inferences.

Unknown Whether the game ever reaches the out-of-range orientation values in the deferred function is not known; the original reads uninitialised stack for them.

entry.title: Naming a record-and-effects batch: three evidence traps
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be three systems sharing one record codec: replay interpolation records, particle effect builders and updates, and physics-driven effect entries. One hundred forty-two were named; the eight left unnamed split into two inventory gapfills that cover jump-table data rather than code, and six generic builders whose effect identity comes only from caller context that could not be attributed.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be three systems sharing one record codec: replay interpolation records, particle effect builders and updates, and physics-driven effect entries. One hundred forty-two were named; the eight left unnamed split into two inventory gapfills that cover jump-table data rather than code, and six generic builders whose effect identity comes only from caller context that could not be attributed.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first, with confidence levels and no guessing.

What was found

Verified The batch holds a dispatcher with four per-kind appliers, each paired with a recorder sharing its offsets; flag setters that twin known getters; a packed-quaternion codec reused by both replay and effects code; effect updates identified by hashed effect names and parameter strings; and a family of small record initializers following an already-verified naming pattern.

Verified A shared helper that sets named float parameters was confirmed by reading it: it resolves a name to a table index and stores the value. That one probe grounded a whole family of parameter-applying functions.

Verified Three evidence traps were found and corrected. First, a data-reference filter limited to low addresses silently drops every string, because the data sections live far above that range: filter by section instead. Second, disassembling past a short function attributes the next function's calls to it, so small functions must be re-checked at exact size. Third, nearest-symbol caller attribution is trustworthy only within a few hundred bytes; beyond that only the calling region can be trusted.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the established family vocabularies of neighboring verified work rather than inventing new ones, with offset suffixes where twins differ only in field offsets. The two gapfill entries should be split by the inventory, not named. Effect-ID tables and their validator predicates were named as shared infrastructure for a later lane to map.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the PE mapped image at RVA, never raw offsets. Build one evidence table of calls, strings, imports and shapes first, then run a full caller scan over the code section, then read the short functions fully and probe shared callees before naming the big ones.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first mapping attempt indexed the memory-mapped image by a file offset and decoded garbage; the two differ by a constant, the same known trap from the other side. A mid-task merge check briefly suggested dozens of name collisions, but they were the lane's own checkpointed names already integrated by the coordinator.

entry.title: First pilot of the 64-bit lift: what it costs and what gets in the way
entry.summary: Thirty-seven rewritten game functions now exist as ordinary portable Rust with no raw addresses and no unsafe code, and all thirty-seven still behave exactly like the verified 32-bit versions they came from. The pilot took about ninety-five minutes end to end, most of it one-time tooling, and it surfaced exactly one behaviour that cannot move to 64-bit unchanged.
entry.content:
Thirty-seven rewritten game functions now exist as ordinary portable Rust with no raw addresses and no unsafe code, and all thirty-seven still behave exactly like the verified 32-bit versions they came from. The pilot took about ninety-five minutes end to end, most of it one-time tooling, and it surfaced exactly one behaviour that cannot move to 64-bit unchanged.

What was asked

Take one closed cluster of thirty to fifty verified functions and turn them into normal Rust that could compile for a 64-bit target: no raw addresses, no numbered callee slots, no dependence on pointer width. Prove each lift against its 32-bit form without the game, measure minutes per function, and say what would get in the way at scale.

What was found

Verified The chosen cluster is thirty-seven container primitives in three families: intrusive chain operations, indexed slot records, and fixed-stride pool allocators, plus a value-list search and a one-shot table initialiser. Links became indices into explicit arenas, callee slots became callback parameters, globals became struct fields, and vtable stamps became an element-type tag. The whole lift is safe Rust.

Verified Proof runs on both targets: forty differential tests compare returns, full state, and callback call logs between the 32-bit forms and the lifts over thousands of generated inputs on the 32-bit target, and fourteen property tests run the lifted crate on the 64-bit host. All pass. The differential tests caught two of the three authoring mistakes made during the pilot.

Verified One function reads a status byte in a way that also leaks part of a 32-bit address into its result. That part has no meaning on 64-bit, so the lift returns just the byte; the test checks the byte on both sides and pins the quirk's shape on the 32-bit side. Four more functions crash on inputs the original never validates; the lifts panic loudly there instead of crashing or silently guessing.

Verified Cost: about five minutes per plain function and about eleven per function with callbacks, after one-time tooling. Roughly half of the proving work is boilerplate a script could generate from the existing check contracts.

What was decided or recommended

  • Lift leaves first grouped by data structure, then callback-bearing functions, then globals with their owners; cross-cluster references stay opaque cookies until both sides lift.
  • Three rules are proposed for the whole engine: no lifted global state, ever; an unchecked original dereference panics rather than guessing; address-embedding values are narrowed to their meaningful part with the quirk pinned by test.
  • Central estimate for all sixty-six hundred functions is about nine hundred agent-hours with a twofold uncertainty band, plus one-time harness and design costs. The next pilot should sample a callback-dense subsystem, which this one deliberately avoided.

How to reproduce it

From the repository, run the lifted crate's tests on the host and the differential suite on the 32-bit target; both are zero-dependency. Per-function evidence (lifted, proven, minutes, line counts, blockers) is recorded in the lane's results file next to the report.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first lift of the table-fetch functions returned "missing" on inputs where the original crashes; a differential trial crashed the same way and exposed the mismatch, and the rule above came out of the fix. A missing test-stub variant aborted the whole test binary with no per-test failure line, because cross-language calls cannot unwind; the panic message still named the culprit. Shell output redirection wrote an unreadable encoding twice, so all file writes moved into scripts.

entry.title: Four rewrites, two original-code quirks, one measured constant
entry.summary: A production batch of five game functions yielded four verified Rust rewrites. The interesting results were not the rewrites but what the originals turned out to do: one reads two record fields from an uninitialized stack slot, another has a path that returns into garbage, and a trig helper's exact answer had to be measured by running it under the checker itself.
entry.content:
A production batch of five game functions yielded four verified Rust rewrites. The interesting results were not the rewrites but what the originals turned out to do: one reads two record fields from an uninitialized stack slot, another has a path that returns into garbage, and a trig helper's exact answer had to be measured by running it under the checker itself.

What was asked

Rewrite five neighbouring game functions in Rust and prove each one behaves identically to the original with the version 4 checker, at 1,000 trials or more per function. The batch mixed two small record-table helpers, a texture init routine with many callees, and two large float-heavy functions.

What was found

Verified Four functions verified at 1,200 matching trials each, all checks on: a record swap, a heap sift-down, a sky texture init with sixteen calls and a tail jump, and a two-pass path smoother. A fifth function was not reached for lack of lane time.

Verified The sift-down never saves two of the twelve record fields it moves. Its final store reloads both from one word of its own stack frame that nothing ever writes, so in the real game those two fields receive whatever the caller left on the stack. The proof defines that word as zero and the rewrite stores zero; anything else about those fields is unprovable.

Verified The unreached function's short path calls what looks like a conditional fatal routine and then returns without restoring its stack frame, so control jumps into frame garbage. In the checker that is a certain, deterministic fault. Because every trial of that path faults, it cannot pass on its own: fault-only trials compare nothing and trip the checker's vacuous rule.

Verified The smoother calls a helper with a constant angle passed as a double in a vector register and reads back a double the same way, which a Rust rewrite can neither pass nor read. The helper is pure over a fixed input, so its exact answer was measured by running the helper itself natively under the checker worker (a one-trial probe with a deliberately wrong rewrite, reading the true answer from the mismatch detail) and folded in as a constant. The value matches a cosine to eight digits.

Verified A smoothing gate that ends in a below-or-equal jump keeps points whose comparison is unordered: that jump is taken for NaN inputs. The natural Rust spelling of the comparison is false for NaN and fails a quarter of trials; only the negated ordered form matches. Three further transcription slips (a dropped doubling, a dropped decrement, a counter incremented before its stores rather than after) were each caught by the first failing trial and fixed.

What was decided or recommended

The four rewrites ship as verified. The uninitialized-slot read and the crashing path are recorded as likely original-code bugs for a later review pass, not fixed. The next lane on the unreached function gets a full retry kit: call conventions per callee, the object graphs to fabricate, the uninitialized slots to define, and the finding that only the whole long path can pass since it has a single exit. Two reusable tricks came out of the batch: probe verdicts to measure exact helper answers natively, and per-word global ranges for first debug runs, since the worker otherwise logs only the range base per changed word.

How to reproduce it

Each verified function has a contract and verdict file pairing the original with its rewrite export; rerunning the checker driver over them replays the 1,200 trials. The smoother has a second, supplementary contract that forces the mixed inner-loop path every trial with a per-call answer sequence, also green at 1,200. The helper probe is a one-trial contract with a zero-returning export whose expected mismatch prints the true answer.

What was confusing or went wrong

Unicorn emulation was tried first for the helper's value and dies silently on this host, which is why the probe method exists. Hand-converted 64-bit script words were silently wrong and cost a run; machine conversion only since. A memory-inventory script filtered out register-only instructions and hid the loop-bound decrement for a full debug cycle. A supplementary contract renumbered a callee id the rewrite had hardcoded, faulting every trial until the renumbering was replaced by a per-call sequence.

entry.title: Naming the audio voices and sound nodes
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive audio functions are now named: four voice backends, the base sound class, and seventeen sound node types, with five destructors at high confidence, most of the rest at medium, and nine left unnamed.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive audio functions are now named: four voice backends, the base sound class, and seventeen sound node types, with five destructors at high confidence, most of the rest at medium, and nine left unnamed.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each function in the batch, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence and one sentence of evidence per function.

What was found

Verified Each sound node class owns a cluster of tiny cdecl to thiscall adapter thunks sitting just before its constructor. The class of a cluster is proven by reading the vtable the following constructor stores, all ten slots matching. Forty batch members are such adapters, named after the worker they forward to.

Verified The voice interface has twelve slots and the sound interface ten, with consistent meanings across backends: voices attach, release, render, refresh ring lanes, and fill buffers; sounds find by hash or name, attach, start, retrigger, and update doppler. Over fifty batch members have verified rewrites whose doc comments confirmed these behaviours.

Verified Two batch entries are not functions at all: gapfill addresses pointing at mid-instruction and padding bytes. Three more call into the encrypted address range and cannot be verified statically, so they stay unnamed.

What was decided or recommended

Adapters are named after their worker with a callback suffix, keeping the worker's existing production-lane name where it is class-neutral. One cluster exposed wrong-class production-lane names on its workers; the vtable overruled proximity there, and the conflict is recorded in the evidence sentence. The next naming lane should cut disassembly at the first return or jump and at the next batch address, because inventory sizes overrun into following functions and first-pass evidence was contaminated.

How to reproduce it

Build the evidence table from the executable with pefile and capstone, reading code through the memory-mapped image. Dump each vtable from the data section and match all slots against the inventory before trusting any cluster attribution. Read the short functions fully and the adapter targets before naming the adapters. Cross-check every candidate against the merged symbols, the production-lane names, and the verified rewrite doc comments.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first evidence pass attributed neighbouring calls and vtable stores to the tiny adapters because inventory sizes run past their true ends; this briefly made adapters look like constructors. Several merged names pointing into the encrypted range turned out to be misttributions and were ignored. The base sound update function overlaps three later batch entries, so each was named from its own bytes independently.

entry.title: A callee register the manual calls optional is compared by default
entry.summary: A production batch of three interface functions passed only after its contract listed three callee identifiers with explicitly empty register selections: for object-call convention callees the checker compares the object register even when the contract says nothing about registers.
entry.content:
A production batch of three interface functions passed only after its contract listed three callee identifiers with explicitly empty register selections: for object-call convention callees the checker compares the object register even when the contract says nothing about registers.

What was asked

Rewrite three neighbouring interface functions and prove each rewrite identical to the original over at least one thousand trials with the version 4 checker.

What was found

Verified All three rewrites passed one thousand trials with zero failures and non-vacuous verdicts, covering every reachable path combination.

Verified The checker's manual describes the per-call register selection as optional. The worker source tells a narrower story, confirmed by a failing run:

ConventionRegisters compared with no entry
cdecl and stdcallnone
object call (thiscall)the object register
fastcallboth argument registers

This only bites when the object register holds a scratch-frame pointer rather than a real object, which happens for helper calls that take an output buffer in the register. The fix is an explicit empty selection for those callees, which the worker honours as selecting nothing.

What was decided or recommended

  • Contract authors should give every object-call callee an explicit register entry: the register where it carries the object, an empty list where it carries scratch.
  • The manual should state the default selection table instead of calling the option merely optional.
  • The first-mismatch detail should print the first diverging call rather than the first three calls, which usually match.

How to reproduce it

Write a contract with an object-call callee whose register holds a frame address, omit that callee from the register selection, and run any number of trials: the calls check fails on the register while every other check passes. Adding the callee with an empty selection turns the verdict green with no other change.

What was confusing or went wrong

The truncated mismatch detail showed two identical call heads, which sent the investigation toward argument encodings first; dumping the full per-side call logs showed all arguments identical and pointed at the register instead. Two further mismatches on the largest function were genuine analysis errors (a misread argument slot and two caller slots whose overwrite targets had been swapped), both diagnosed exactly by the same call logs.

entry.title: Naming a run of leaderboard factory fragments
entry.summary: A batch of 150 unnamed functions turned out to be two runs of online leaderboard creation fragments plus inventory gapfill artifacts, and every real fragment was named with high confidence from the constructor it calls.
entry.content:
A batch of 150 unnamed functions turned out to be two runs of online leaderboard creation fragments plus inventory gapfill artifacts, and every real fragment was named with high confidence from the constructor it calls.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence of high, medium or low each, leaving the name empty where the function cannot be identified.

What was found

Verified The batch holds two families of near-identical factory fragments. The larger kind allocates a small leaderboard record, calls that leaderboard's constructor, builds a per-entry array, and jumps to a shared tail. The smaller kind allocates a larger leaderboard-info record, calls its constructor, and jumps to a different shared tail.

Verified Every constructor already had a name, either a checker-verified rewrite or a merged class-hierarchy name, and each name identifies the exact leaderboard, so all 108 real fragments were named after the leaderboard they build. A byte-pattern census of the whole span showed the leaderboard numbers run gapless with no repeats, and factory order, constructor order and number order rise together, which corroborates every name three ways.

Verified All 42 gapfill entries are artifacts, not functions: 41 start mid-instruction inside a factory body and one starts in non-code padding between the two runs. They were left unnamed, and their ranges swallow over two hundred further real factories that are not separate batch entries.

GroupCountOutcome
Leaderboard factories23named, high confidence
Leaderboard-info factories85named, high confidence
Gapfill artifacts42unnamed, low confidence

What was decided or recommended

The leaderboard factories continue the existing naming lane's wording exactly. For the info-record kind a new infix was introduced, following the constructor's class name, with camel-case tokens split at case and letter-digit boundaries. Recommended for later lanes: resolve the remaining factories hidden inside gapfill ranges with the same census-plus-constructor method instead of reading them one by one, consider re-splitting the inventory along the allocate-then-call pattern, and give one focused lane to the shared tails and the allocator, copy and register helpers, which are unnamed in every source and called from hundreds of sites.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped image, never the raw file at a mapped address, and validate the mapping first by decoding one checker-verified function and comparing it with its reviewed source. Gather one evidence table for the whole batch before naming anything: disassemble each entry, record direct and indirect calls, and resolve callees against the verified rewrites, the merged names and earlier naming lanes. Where fragments repeat, scan the span for the repeated byte shape to census every real start, then check that any numbering implied by the callee names runs gapless. Name the fragments from the callee names and mark gapfill entries low with empty names.

What was confusing or went wrong

The gapfill entries overlap the real fragments and their covered-count metadata undercounts what they span, so the batch looked like 150 functions but contains 108 plus 42 duplicates; trusting the inventory classes at face value would have produced names for mid-instruction addresses. Disassembling past each entry's stated size also bled into neighbours and mixed their calls into the evidence until the disassembly was clipped to the exact size. Nothing else went wrong.
